title: Yaki Onigiri
subtitle: grilled soy-glazed rice balls
excerpt: Yaki onigiri are rice balls pressed flat and grilled in a pan until the outside is crispy, then brushed with soy sauce and mirin and grilled again until the glaze caramelises. They are deeply savoury and very satisfying. Makes 8 rice balls.
sourceNotes: Yaki onigiri are popular at yakitori restaurants and Japanese barbecue joints where they are grilled over charcoal. The charcoal versions have a smoky crust that is hard to replicate at home, but a dry cast iron pan gets very close.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch of plain onigiri and grill to order.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Shape the rice balls up to 2 hours ahead. Grill just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: Japanese hand-pressed rice balls. Yaki onigiri are the grilled version, pressed firmly and cooked until the outside forms a crispy crust.
Sweet Japanese rice wine. Mixed with soy sauce to make the glaze for yaki onigiri. It caramelises quickly under heat and gives the glaze its characteristic shine.

content.text: are grilled in a dry pan until the rice forms a crust, then brushed with a soy and
glaze and grilled again. The key is not adding any oil to the pan. The starch on the outside of the rice ball must be allowed to crust directly on the dry surface. Makes 8.
Press the rice balls firmly into a flat triangular or oval shape before grilling. Loose rice balls will fall apart when you try to flip them.
Wet your hands and press the warm rice into 8 tightly packed triangles or oval shapes. Each should be about 80g. Press firmly: they need to be dense and compact.
Mix the soy sauce, mirin and sesame oil together in a small bowl.
Heat a cast iron skillet over medium heat with no oil. Place the rice balls flat-side down. Do not move them. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the underside is golden and forms a crust.

Flip carefully with a thin spatula. Cook the second side for 3 to 4 minutes. Brush the top with the soy glaze. Flip and brush the other side. Cook for 1 more minute per side until the glaze is dark and caramelised.
Remove from the pan. Scatter with sesame seeds if using. Serve immediately while the crust is still crispy.

attrs.symptom: Rice ball sticks to the pan and breaks apart
attrs.cause: Pan was not hot enough or the rice ball was moved before the crust formed
attrs.fix: Heat the pan well before adding the rice balls. Do not touch them for a full 3 minutes. The crust will release naturally.

attrs.cause: Glaze was applied when the heat was too high
attrs.fix: Reduce the heat to medium-low before brushing on the glaze. The mirin sugar burns very quickly over high heat.

attrs.cause: Rice was too wet when formed, or the ball was not pressed firmly enough
attrs.fix: Use freshly cooked rice that has steamed dry. Press firmly so the rice is compact before grilling.

content.text: Yaki onigiri are served at yakitori stalls and izakaya as a dish to finish the meal. Eating a rice ball at the end of a yakitori meal is a Japanese tradition. The grilled soy crust gives a completely different texture from a plain onigiri. At home they are a brilliant way to use leftover cooked rice. The cast iron pan does exactly the same job as a charcoal grill.
